Black Box Warning Conjugated estrogens (oral) are FDA-approved for the treatment of vasomotor symptoms due to menopause, vulvar and vaginal atrophy due to menopause, hypogonadism, castration, primary ovarian failure, palliative treatment of breast cancer, and androgen-dependent prostate carcinoma. This medication carries a Black Box Warning, which highlights significant risks associated with its use. Common Adverse Reactions Frequently reported side effects include edema, vasodilation, chloasma, hirsutism, injection site reactions, pruritus, weight changes, abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, flatulence, nausea, vomiting, backache, leg cramps, asthenia, headache, migraine, depression, mood disturbances, menstrual disorders, breast pain, vaginitis, withdrawal bleeding, cough, and pharyngitis. Adult Indications and Dosage FDA-Labeled Indications and Dosage (Adults) Treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms due to menopause. Treatment of moderate to severe vulvar and vaginal atrophy due to menopause. For these symptoms, topical vaginal products should be considered. Treatment of hypoestrogenism due to hypogonadism, castration, or primary ovarian failure. Palliative treatment of breast cancer in appropriately selected patients with metastatic disease. Palliative treatment of advanced androgen-dependent prostate carcinoma. Prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis. This therapy should only be considered for women at significant risk of osteoporosis and for whom non-estrogen medications are not appropriate. General Guidelines For postmenopausal osteoporosis prevention, weight-bearing exercise, adequate calcium (1,500 mg/day), and vitamin D (400–800 IU/day) intake are essential. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation may be helpful for women with suboptimal dietary intake. When prescribing estrogen for a postmenopausal woman with a uterus, progestin should also be initiated to reduce the risk of endometrial cancer. Women without a uterus do not require progestin. Estrogen therapy should be administered at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with treatment goals and individual risks. Patients should be periodically reevaluated (e.g., every 3–6 months) to determine if continued treatment is necessary. Contraindications Conjugated estrogens should not be used in individuals with the following conditions: Undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding. Known, suspected, or history of breast cancer (except in selected metastatic cases). Known or suspected estrogen-dependent neoplasia. Active or history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism. Active or recent arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction). Liver dysfunction or disease. Known hypersensitivity to any ingredients in the medication. Known or suspected pregnancy. Warnings Estrogen-alone therapy has been associated with an increased risk of stroke and DVT. Estrogen plus progestin therapy has been associated with an increased risk of stroke, DVT, pulmonary embolism, and myocardial infarction. If any of these events occur or are suspected, discontinue estrogen therapy immediately. Risk factors for arterial vascular disease (e.g., hypertension, diabetes, smoking, hypercholesterolemia, obesity) and venous thromboembolism (e.g., personal or family history of VTE, obesity, systemic lupus erythematosus) should be managed appropriately. In the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) studies, estrogen-alone and estrogen-plus-progestin therapies were associated with increased risks of stroke and VTE. These risks were evident early in treatment and persisted. Adverse Reactions Adverse reactions reported with estrogen and/or progestin therapy include: Abnormal uterine bleeding, dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, and changes in cervical secretions. Breast tenderness, enlargement, pain, discharge, and fibrocystic changes. Increased risk of breast cancer, endometrial hyperplasia, and endometrial cancer. Venous thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, and stroke. Nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, bloating, and gallbladder disease. Skin reactions such as chloasma, erythema multiforme, and alopecia. Headache, migraine, mood disturbances, and dementia. Weight changes, glucose intolerance, and exacerbation of asthma or epilepsy. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy Conjugated estrogens should not be used during pregnancy. Nursing Mothers Estrogen administration to nursing mothers may reduce the quantity and quality of breast milk. Detectable amounts of estrogen have been identified in breast milk. Pediatric Use Estrogen therapy has been used to induce puberty in adolescents with delayed puberty. Geriatric Use There is insufficient data to determine whether geriatric patients respond differently to conjugated estrogens compared to younger patients.
